newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE to boycott Mideast summit if peace talks stall.
newsitem.headline: UAE to boycott Mideast summit if peace talks stall.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates said on Sunday it would boycott a controversial Arab-Israeli economic conference in Qatar in the absence of any signs of a breakthrough in the Middle East peace talks.
"Our attendance is conditional," Information Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zaid al-Nahayan told Reuters. "If there is no progress (in the peace talks) we will not attend the summit."

Qatar, strongly backed by Washington, has said it was going ahead with preparations for the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) annual economic summit in November regardless of pressure from other Arab states to cancel or postpone it.

Washington had earlier suggested to Qatar to split the summit events between several venues in the Gulf, allowing participants to visit several of the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states, diplomats said.
The GCC includes Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman.

But with two GCC members -- Saudi Arabia and the UAE -- publicly saying they would boycott the meeting, others are expected to follow suit unless they see a change in Israeli policies, Gulf officials said.
"Haggling in the peace talks is one thing but Jerusalem is another matter. It is not just a Palestinian issue or an Arab one," said a Gulf official.

Arab states, which accuse Israel of stalling the peace process, are extremely worried about what they see as aggressive measures to change the face of Jerusalem -- a city also holy to Moslems -- while they say Washington is failing to exert any pressure on the Jewish state.
Regional powerbroker Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally, was the first Gulf state to announce it would not attend the summit and has urged Qatar to cancel it.

Gulf sources said Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Abdullah had discussed the issue with a Qatari envoy late last month, expressing strong displeasure with Doha's insistence to go ahead with the summit despite strong Arab objections.

The GCC states, Egypt and Syria are expected to discuss the issue at a ministerial meeting in September. Syria has boycotted the previous three MENA summits and has urged Arab states to do the same this year.
"Qatar's insistence is making things worse," said a Gulf source of an apparent decision by some GCC states to drop earlier compromise solutions in favour of a boycott.
Some were considering sending a low level delegation in a face-saving move or a senior GCC official to represent all six.
Kuwait, another close Washington ally, has said it would decide on its stand once it receives an official invitation from Qatar but Kuwait's parliament has called for a boycott.
